title: When ICE Comes for a MAGA Supporter
excerpt: Last year, the conservative evangelical blogger Samuel Sey published an article on his blog, Slow to Write, defending the Trump administration’s plan for mass d
body: Last year, the conservative evangelical blogger Samuel Sey published an article on his blog, Slow to Write, defending the Trump administration’s plan for mass deportations from a Christian perspective. “Christian ethics do not denounce deportations,” he wrote. “They demand it.” Born in Ghana and a resident of Canada before he moved to the United States, Sey went on to write that “America doesn’t owe anything to people born outside of the country—including me.” Last week, on October 21, ICE arrested Sey, who now faces deportation from the United States––a devastating blow to his American-born wife and three American children
A DHS spokesperson called Sey “an illegal alien” in a statement to news outlets

A statement attributed to Sey’s wife asserts that he entered the U.S. legally “and has been working ever since in good faith with a lawyer to obtain permanent legal status.” Some of his supporters have blamed his arrest on a clerical error. (The DHS spokesperson claimed in the statement that the 39-year-old Sey overstayed his legal entry by four years.) Arrests of this sort are nothing new in most respects
Federal-enforcement efforts in the United States’ interior have recently averaged 19,000 deportations a month
Although some deportees are doubtless unsympathetic criminals, many thousands are good people with families or friends who suffer their absence acutely
Sey is unusual, however, in being known personally to many prominent MAGA-aligned Christians, some of whom have backed a fundraiser for his family and affirmed his good character
That support has angered some within the MAGA coalition
A prevailing MAGA narrative is Illegal immigrants are members of a lawless, untrustworthy out-group that is justly hated for the significant harm that it does to America

That narrative is threatened when a member of the MAGA in-group, whose personal and professional life many MAGA allies affirmed as good for America, is accused of being an “illegal alien.” Perhaps that’s why the debate about Sey’s arrest has been so polarizing, and why MAGA participants are finding it harder than usual to ignore the complexities of the issue and the fissures in their coalition
Joel Berry, who has described himself as “a right-wing protestant conservative evangelical Christian Trump supporter,” is the person who created a crowdfunding effort for Sey and his family

In past commentary, Berry has called for a moratorium on U.S. immigration; stated that “if we’re going to save America, it won’t be enough to deport all the migrants”; and argued that “there’s no such thing as an ‘illegal immigrant with no criminal record’ because illegal immigration is a crime.” He once asserted that “the only due process owed to an illegal alien is deportation.” The crowdfunding appeal he launched states of Sey: “His wife is working to get him released on bail so he can fix any clerical issues that need to be addressed for his legal residence

We are raising money to help his wife and children with expenses while he’s out of work, as well as any legal fees they incur.” It concludes, “Samuel is a good man and a brother in Christ, and his ministry at SlowToWrite has been a blessing to many
Thank you for standing with them!” Many in the MAGA coalition criticized Berry for standing with someone they believe to be a lawbreaker
In response, Berry stated both that “Samuel Sey is in my tribe, and he is my brother

And he would make an excellent American,” and that “I of course believe the law should be enforced no matter who it involves.” The due process that Berry has previously dismissed is exactly what could determine whether his friend was arrested because of a clerical error or because he was in fact here unlawfully

The debate has altered Berry’s perception of his coalition’s moral character. “This has been probably the darkest 24 hours I’ve ever experienced on social media,” he wrote . “The things being said about Samuel, his wife, and his small children are unthinkably evil
There is a segment of the so-called ‘Christian’ nationalist crowd that has given itself completely over to Satan

I’ve never had more resolve to defeat these subversive demons invading the Right and invading Christianity.” Allie Beth Stuckey, a Christian conservative podcaster for Blaze Media and the author of Toxic Empathy: How Progressives Exploit Christian Compassion , has criticized what she sees as “toxic empathy” in the immigration debate

People are “so focused on the hard journey of the migrant that it belittles the effect of the chaos of illegal immigration on children, innocent citizens, and victims of illegal immigrant crime,” she wrote

In her telling, “Being so empathetic toward one set of people that you’re blinded to everyone and everything else isn’t just misguided, it’s evil.” But in Sey’s case, she urged her followers to understand and connect with his family’s feelings and perspective. “As you can imagine, his wife, who’s at home with their 3 babies, is devastated and also trusting the Lord to help them find a resolution quickly,” she wrote. “Please pray for all of the Seys.” Megan Basham of The Daily Wire , who is also a conservative Christian, posted this after learning that Sey had been detained: “I have spoken to people close to my friend Sam Sey, and this is not a question of any deliberate law breaking
Anyone saying otherwise is not telling you the truth

And anyone rejoicing over his and his precious wife Annie’s difficulties in this situation is disgusting.” I was struck by the contrast with a social-media exchange I had with Basham earlier this month, when I was critiquing the Trump administration for deporting dozens of Venezuelan men to a brutally abusive prison in El Salvador

She was defending it. “Should overstaying your visa in the United States carry the risk of being beaten and sexually assaulted by sadistic prison guards in a foreign dictatorship where you’ve never set foot, paid for by the US government?” I asked her , adding, “I don’t think it should carry that risk
I don’t think Jesus would think it should carry that risk either.” She replied , “Yes, because you should go home when your visa expires

If you don’t, you’re breaking the law and you run the risk of whatever penalties come along with that.” Some commentators in the MAGA coalition seem to adopt rhetoric and positions on illegal immigration that they can maintain only when they think of illegal immigrants as an abstract “them.” When they confront one who is a concrete “us,” their rhetoric shifts significantly

They raise rather than ignore the possibility of procedural errors, extoll the value of due process, note personal circumstances, draw attention to the suffering of family members, and urge empathy rather than vilification
Others in the MAGA coalition object to this shift
Some are bigots who use racial slurs in their posts or attack interracial couples such as Sey and his wife
Others are restrictionists who believe that mass deportations are necessary and will cease if illegal immigrants are humanized and shown empathy

I wonder how many of those attacking Sey and his humanizers are those who are triggered by the simple cognitive dissonance of hearing good things about a person who may belong to categories such as “illegal alien” or “lawbreaker”—categories that they are accustomed to coding as evil
Many in the MAGA movement hope that uncompromising harshness toward all undocumented immigrants will result in maximizing the number of people whom the country is able to deport

But the longer that the mass deportation of otherwise law-abiding people persists, the harder it will be to maintain support for that approach: Rather than assume that deportees are mostly villains, more and more people will have personal connections to productive members of society who got deported

Why does immigration law require someone who marries an American to spend years filling out onerous paperwork with catastrophic penalties for errors? Wouldn’t Americans benefit if the law drew more distinctions between, for example, a visa overstay by a gainfully employed, noncriminal father of American children and a serial perpetrator of violence who twice snuck into the country? A movement that genuinely prioritizes the interests of U.S. citizens would have better answers to such questions than Trump, whose approach is deportations first, not “America first.”

title: Flying Across the World to Vote
excerpt: Photographs and videos by Dana Golan Since the beginning of the Gaza war, a record number of Israelis have left the country
body: Photographs and videos by Dana Golan Since the beginning of the Gaza war, a record number of Israelis have left the country

More than 10 percent of the electorate now lives abroad, and the country generally does not allow absentee ballots: Those who want to vote in today’s election, the first since October 7, need to be there in person
An estimated 67,000 Israeli expats have traveled thousands of miles—and spent thousands of dollars—to return home
Within Israel, the polls suggest a fairly even split between the parties that favor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and those that oppose him
But most of the expats are expected to support the opposition
The prime minister’s allies reportedly considered restricting airport capacity to limit the number of arrivals
Israelis returning from abroad expressed feelings of deep investment in this election and a belief that the outcome will affect them no matter where they live
Many are willing to travel a long way to vote for what they believe will be a better future

Dana Golan for The Atlantic Maya Mor Mitrani, a college student and opera singer in Philadelphia, spoke about concern for her father, who has served in the military reserves since October 7. “I just think the situation is really bad,” she said, “and I want to have at least some influence over how the government tries to solve the problems we’re facing right now
So if my influence amounts to just one ballot in the box, that’s what I’ll do.” Dana Golan for The Atlantic Jonathan Matkowsky was born in America, but he moved to Israel in 2012
On October 7, he barricaded his children indoors and drove south to help however he could, working as a volunteer driver for off-duty soldiers and civilians for the next four months
Now he has returned for the election: “It’s a meaningful vote for me because of how much trauma we’ve been through,” he said
Although he considered voting for Gadi Eisenkot because of his support for extending the draft to the ultra-Orthodox, he ultimately decided to vote for Netanyahu
He trusts the prime minister’s wisdom and experience and credits him with keeping Israel safe: “I’m proud of him
Dana Golan for The Atlantic New York’s John F
Kennedy International Airport on October 25, 2026 Dana Golan for The Atlantic A banner that reads “This time, Eisenkot” hangs in Jaffa, Tel Aviv
Dana Golan for The Atlantic An organization called Fly&Vote organized expats to fly from New York to Tel Aviv on October 25
Dana Golan for The Atlantic Shirily Bar-Or spent years protesting in Israel before moving to Athens last year. “I didn’t give up, exactly
I hope I’ll be able to breathe again tomorrow.” What she wants, she said, is for “the country to be sane again
I want a government that works for the public good

I want democracy.” To her this election is pivotal because, she said, what Netanyahu wants “is to destroy us just to save his own skin.” Dana Golan for The Atlantic Dan Galezer lives in New York and already had a trip to Israel planned, but he changed his flight to be there on Election Day
He said that he didn’t know which opposition party to support, but that “I’m just at the stage of saying: Get Bibi out of the seat already

His time is up.” Galezer’s family’s kibbutz was the site of one of the worst massacres on October 7. “Today, even after everything that’s happened,” he said, “I don’t rule out returning.” But whether that will even be possible, he said, may depend on the outcome of the election: “This feels like a breaking point.” Dana Golan for The Atlantic Arie Deizer has lived in Bucharest for 30 years and compared Netanyahu to the Hungarian strongman Viktor Orbán

Netanyahu, he said, has “destroyed the country—he’s completely lost it now,” and Deizer hopes he’ll be “thrown out, just like Orbán.” Deizer is voting for the Democrats, in part because unlike many other opposition parties, they have not ruled out working with Arab parties should they win. “I hope we’ll have an overwhelming majority here—70 seats—so that the Arab parties can’t be ignored.” Dana Golan for The Atlantic A sign on the entrance to a shop in Jaffa, Tel Aviv, reads “Jews and Arabs refuse to be enemies.” Dana Golan for The Atlantic Shai Sinai hasn’t lived in Israel for 40 years, but he’s come back from Hamburg to vote in every election since Netanyahu came to power. “I was born here, I grew up here, I was educated here, I served in the army here, and my whole family—the family members who are still alive—basically lives here.” Volunteers from Fly&Vote, a nonprofit dedicated to helping expats return for the election, met him and other voters at the airport
So did members of the Democrats, a party Sinai said he will support

He hopes that the government will be replaced, he said, but “to say that I’m expecting it would be too optimistic.” Dana Golan for The Atlantic Volunteers and candidates from the Democrats Party came to greet Israelis as they landed in Israel to vote
Dana Golan for The Atlantic Election posters at the entrance to a polling station in Tel Aviv include one from Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad party that reads “We Will Only Fix This Together.”

title: Who Said It: Marissa Mayer, or Odysseus?
excerpt: Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task
body: Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task
Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special
Mayer—the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer—likes cracking a hard problem
But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers
So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle
Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said

In an attempt to express the blend of bewilderment and despair brought on by this New York Times anecdote , I have concocted a quiz: Which is it—a question the tech industry wants me to ask AI, or something Odysseus asks upon returning to Ithaca after 20 years of absence? Tell me, what is my son like? Who are these people in my house? Are any of these people my son’s friends? Are any of these people my friends? What makes my son smile? What would make a good gift for my son? Do I have anything in common with my son? Would archery be a fun activity to do to impress my family? Is there a quicker route home I could take next time? What would be a nifty surprise for my wife? What activities or items does my wife enjoy? What activity can I do to bond with my wife and son? Does my dog recognize me? Is there something I can feed my elderly dog that will help him live longer? I am told this is my home, but I don’t recognize any of these people in my house, and I don’t know what they want
I am told this is my life, but all of the intimate things that should be the most familiar feel foreign to me
Suggest a fun activity to distract me from the terrifying sense that I have hollowed out my life with my own hands, and that my absence has filled my house with strangers! Is Zendaya Athena?

title: The Limits of Trump’s Midterm Trickery
excerpt: For the first time in modern American history, a sitting president is seeking to wield the force of the state to secure an electoral victory for his party
body: For the first time in modern American history, a sitting president is seeking to wield the force of the state to secure an electoral victory for his party

The Trump administration has attempted to undermine the widespread use of mail-in voting; demanded that states hand over voter rolls; threatened to prosecute state and local election officials; refused to rule out the idea of deploying troops or federal agents to polling places; and publicized the dramatic arrests of small numbers of people accused of voting or registering to vote as noncitizens

Many of these efforts have made little headway—either because of the administration’s incompetence, the stubborn lack of factual evidence behind President Trump’s claims of voter fraud, the federal government’s lack of legal authority, or the refusal of courts to go along with Trump’s plans
But Trump may have a different problem on his hands
Polls show Trump’s approval falling to all-time lows in the weeks before Election Day; the percent of voters happy with his performance has now sunk into the 30s
Democrats, meanwhile, appear likely to retake control of the House of Representatives and maybe even the Senate, which last year seemed well out of reach
The polls could be wrong—and high-profile-polling misses of the Trump era are hard to forget
But if the polling is right, the GOP may be in for what George W

Bush, after a disastrous 2006 midterm, ruefully termed a “thumping.” And a thumping, as opposed to a narrower Democratic victory, could render most efforts to suppress turnout irrelevant, and make it far more difficult to implement any more dramatic effort to rig the results
To Trump’s endless frustration, elections in America are organized at the state and local level, with little role for the federal government
In a typical midterm year, almost 470 congressional seats are up for grabs across 50 different states

Though a small number of those races are actually competitive, tinkering with the outcome of the votes would still require meddling with a number of different elections, all run differently, in different jurisdictions, under different laws

A strong night for the Democratic Party would make conjuring an ersatz House majority hard for the same reason that a losing sports team is less able to cheat its way to a victory in a blowout. (Even on a very strong night for the Democrats, the Senate may still be quite a close call.) Tight margins, by contrast, can make an election more vulnerable to efforts to undo the voters’ will
Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 presidential election relied in significant part on tight margins in some swing states, sometimes with only 10,000 or 20,000 votes deciding the winner
In Georgia, the president famously pushed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to make up his deficit against Joe Biden

As described by both the House January 6 committee’s report and Jack Smith’s indictment of Trump, Trump and his allies used close tallies in swing states, together with the slow counting of mail-in ballots, to engineer doubts over election results and provide Republican members of Congress with the tools to delay the formal counting of the electoral vote on January 6

The memory of January 6, and the entrenchment of the election-denier movement since 2020, has led to speculation—both anxious and enthused—about the possibility of a comparable attack on election results in 2026

If, once most of the results are in, Democrats seem set to eke out a House majority by just a few seats, perhaps committed Trump allies in positions of power could make trouble in a handful of the closest districts

A local election commissioner, say, could refuse to sign off on a Democrat’s narrow victory, or the Justice Department could execute a warrant to seize ballots and thus delay or upend the counting of votes

This could create chaos on January 3, when the new House gathers for the first time: What happens if the contested seats are enough to deny the should-be-majority party the votes it needs to select a new speaker and take control of the chamber? Although this isn’t a foolproof trick for stealing control of the House, such a play could make things very precarious very quickly

But the bigger the majority secured by Democrats, the more difficult it would be for Trump to shave that majority down—the more clerks to convince, warrants to secure, and court rulings to dodge, all over the country. “If there is a House majority in either direction that is 20, 30 seats, I think the likelihood of an attempt to engage in some kind of shenanigans around January 3 is way less than if the majority is two or three seats,” Jonathan Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center commented recently on a preelection panel convened at UCLA’s law school
Other tricks are also less effective when the vote swings heavily in one direction
For example, Trump’s unprecedented push for explicitly partisan off-cycle redistricting may net only a few extra GOP seats rather than the double-digit gains Democratic strategists had once feared

Any scheme to steal the House for the GOP would depend on the willingness of congressional Republicans to vote in lockstep, with no defectors—something that the current fractious House Republican caucus can barely manage
Already, though, Republicans spooked by Trump’s bad poll numbers have begun distancing themselves from him on the campaign trail as they fight to hold on to their seats
Over the summer, Republican politicians and MAGA-friendly media outlets responded coolly to a rambling address by the president casting doubt on election integrity

If the GOP loses the House, how many Republicans concerned about their own political careers would be actually inclined to adopt the fringe message of an ever more unpopular lame-duck president? (Trump has been notably quiet recently about the possibility of running for an unconstitutional third term.) Trump will be hard-pressed to fight against “a clear loss, coupled with the expectation of a clear loss,” Bob Bauer told me

Bauer—a longtime Democratic lawyer who played a central role in the Biden campaign’s fight against Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election—now focuses on bipartisan election-integrity work, alongside Ben Ginsberg, an election lawyer known for his past work representing the Republican Party
In 2020, Bauer said, the additional days required for the presidential race to be called after the polls closed helped fuel Trump’s claims of fraud

But now, broad public dissatisfaction has aligned with dismal polling for the GOP and a growing anticipation among both politicians and the press that Republicans will do poorly. “It would be very difficult in these circumstances, if things turn out that the Democrats do well, for him to suddenly announce that he was denied his landslide by vote rigging,” Bauer told me
Just because such a scheme would be implausible does not, of course, mean that Trump won’t try it

Last week, the Justice Department filed a bizarre lawsuit seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate race—but only if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses. (“The legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen,” wrote the law professor Derek Muller in an analysis of the case.) DOJ also continues to pursue litigation seeking to force California to set aside mail-in ballots to voters whom the federal government claims to have identified as noncitizens
These cases are sloppy, tardy, and almost certainly doomed
But they do have the advantage of helping Trump and his allies build a narrative about the courts blocking Trump’s efforts to ensure a fair election

Likewise, if a Trump-aligned rogue local election official tried to block a Democratic candidate’s victory, whatever he or she concocted as reasoning could provide fuel for election-fraud rumors on the far right, even if the effort—as it likely would—ultimately failed
In a wave election, some races will still be close
They may just be in different states or districts—mostly, more Republican ones—than in a year with more typical political geography
House seats in deep-red areas across the country may be newly up for grabs
In the Senate, races in Texas and Alaska stand out as potential flash points. “Any close race in the Senate is going to be hotly, hotly contested,” Bauer told me

He pointed to the bitter fight between the Democrat Al Franken and the Republican Norm Coleman over the 2008 Senate election in Minnesota, which took months to resolve and ended with the courts upholding Franken’s 312-vote victory

title: The Illusion of ‘Radical Transparency’
excerpt: One of the curiosities of Donald Trump’s enduring (if perhaps weakening) grip on his supporters is how they praise him as someone who “tells it like it is.” Tru
body: One of the curiosities of Donald Trump’s enduring (if perhaps weakening) grip on his supporters is how they praise him as someone who “tells it like it is.” Trump’s gatekeepers have similarly declared this to be “the most transparent administration in history,” pointing to, among other things, Trump’s willingness to open his sycophantic Cabinet meetings to live media coverage as proof that nothing is being obscured
The irony of this, of course, is that Trump has been caught in more obvious lies than any president in history
Yet by making himself so ubiquitous, Trump breeds an illusion of openness

To him, a president’s ultimate power rests in his ability to always be in people’s faces—to become inescapable, if not honestly examined; to impose his own self-serving version of reality whenever he pleases, no matter how outlandish
I kept thinking about this as I watched You Can See Everything , the blockbuster documentary that has become a source of cultural fascination since it started packing theaters a few weeks ago
This might be my Trump Derangement Syndrome showing, but I couldn’t help but view the film as a classic Trump-era parable

You Can See Everything chronicles the disgraced Theranos founder, Elizabeth Holmes, and her fiancé, Billy Evans, during their final 34 days together, with their two young children, before Holmes begins an 11-year prison sentence for criminal fraud

In the opening scene, Evans introduces the promise of “radical transparency.” The couple have invited the filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into their beachside rental house near San Diego

In Evans’s telling, the false narrative of Holmes as a scheming con artist has become so entrenched that they might as well raise every curtain, and allow people see her at this most vulnerable and unguarded time
They have nothing to lose and nothing to hide. [ Read: Can Elizabeth Holmes drop the act? ] Like Trump, Holmes and Evans are rich, famous, and secure in their victimhood
No one should have to go through this , as Trump often says (“no one” meaning himself)
Holmes’s aura cries out for caretaking, and not just by Evans, who assumes the role aggressively, or deviously
Her voice goes from insistent monotone at the start to plaintive and soft as her banishment approaches
Everything has been taken from her, unfairly
Like the president, Holmes is adept at playing to reality-TV sensibilities
She seems to have an intuitive sense for when a flash of frustration or vexation can enhance a scene
The camera loves her, even (or especially) when she is melting down
Holmes recognizes the hypnotic effect of her sad, toddlerlike eyes. “It took me a really long time to be okay with letting someone see me cry,” she confides to Fielder, and then sheds a tear on cue
Holmes operates not so much with words as with complete denial that she has intentionally hurt anyone
At one point, she claims that she’s never told a lie in her life
And how can anyone doubt her? We can see everything, after all, so maybe the problem is ours
That is the power of radical transparency
It can breed confusion in us, the audience, rather than clarity about the subject
Fielder, who manages to convey a presence that is both empathetic and dubious, keeps suggesting that Evans and Holmes are not on the level
As the story unfolds, their promise of radical transparency unravels
It becomes evident that Evans is restricting access, manipulating facts, and perhaps exploiting what’s left of his partner’s marketable image
Over the course of the film, Holmes’s responses to Fielder’s inquiries become mushy pleas of ignorance and confusion
If she is guilty of anything, she seems to suggest, it is of allowing herself to be badly misunderstood
She has erred not morally or legally, but in how she’s communicated

Politicians are always doing this too, placing blame not on their own shortcomings but on their (and their staff’s) failure to properly convey the greatness they’ve achieved. [ Idrees Kahloon: Theranos-style fraud has become the norm ] Many of Silicon Valley’s most charismatic entrepreneurs are skilled at creating belief systems, around their products and themselves, as my colleague David Sims wrote in his review of You Can See Everything
Steve Jobs, the Apple co-founder, is considered the virtuoso of this
She wore the same black turtlenecks and intense gaze, and modeled her seductive corporate persona after his (notwithstanding that, unlike Theranos, Apple makes products that actually work)
Watching leaders—political or corporate—who project total faith in their ability to persuade and inspire can be mesmerizing
They are convinced that just by getting in front of an audience, they can bring viewers around, no matter what they say or what they are selling
Trump has at times taken his own confidence to absurd extremes
Early on in the coronavirus pandemic, he insisted on near-daily press conferences
He had no grasp of the viral menace at hand but seemed to believe that his presence alone could transcend the scary science
He might have made little sense, but he did so with total conviction
And he made himself so relentlessly visible
That had to be reassuring, right? One of Trump’s superpowers has been his ability to outlast his skeptics

title: Bernie Sanders Thinks the Democratic Party Is Moving Toward Him
excerpt: A s the Bernie Sanders road show traveled south through Maine earlier this month, the crowds grew bigger and louder with each stop
body: A s the Bernie Sanders road show traveled south through Maine earlier this month, the crowds grew bigger and louder with each stop
About 650 people showed up at a convention center in Bangor, then 700 packed a former church in Lewiston, and finally more than 1,000 filled a high-school gymnasium in Biddeford
Sanders was stumping for Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate, and the faithful were nodding along to the hits
He pitched Medicare for All and raising taxes on billionaires
He decried wealth disparities (“an obscenity”) and Donald Trump (“the most dangerous president” in American history) with equal fervor
What was surprising about Sanders’s appearance in the middle of one of the nation’s hardest-fought Senate races was less what he said and more that he was there at all
Mid-October in an election year is not usually Sanders’s busy season
The Vermont senator last had a tough race in his home state during President Bill Clinton’s first term

And although Sanders can draw a crowd like few other progressive politicians, Democratic candidates typically embrace him during primaries and then stick him on the sideline for the stretch run, when they’re rediscovering their love of capitalism and bipartisanship
This fall, however, Sanders is in far more demand than usual

He’s campaigning for Democrats in some of the most competitive battlegrounds, entrusted not only with juicing turnout on college campuses—his assigned role in earlier years—but with persuading voters in Republican-leaning areas as well
From Maine, Sanders headed to Florida and then on to Texas and Michigan

That Sanders finds himself, a decade after his first run for the presidency, arguably at the peak of his influence is all the more remarkable given that he recently turned 85 and that Democrats have spent the past two years wringing their hands over their party’s gerontocracy
According to YouGov , Sanders is the most popular current elected official in America—only the retirees Barack Obama and Arnold Schwarzenegger have higher ratings

Many of this year’s primary candidates whom Sanders backed defeated establishment opponents in states and districts that Trump had carried in 2024, and they now appear poised to help Democrats retake a majority in the House, and possibly the Senate

And when the party’s 2028 presidential free-for-all kicks off, Sanders’s endorsement could be among the campaign’s most sought-after prizes. “He will be seen as one of the most consequential political leaders of the 21st century,” Representative Ro Khanna of California, one of several Democrats who are likely to try to carry the Sanders mantle to the White House, told me. (Whether offering such high praise will help win Sanders’s nod is another question.) Khanna noted that Sanders’s appeal may be on the upswing precisely because he’s not running for office, and unless he intends to stay in the Senate into his mid-90s, he is unlikely to do so again

But in interviews over the past few weeks, candidates, strategists, and voters across the political spectrum attributed Sanders’s sudden October relevance to the mainstreaming of ideas that he has championed for years
Attacks on big corporations are now a hallmark of both parties
As many as two-thirds of American voters support Sanders’s signature Medicare for All proposal, long derided by Republicans as socialized medicine, according to a recent poll

Democrats who were stung by a second loss to Trump are rethinking their assumptions about what the public really wants. “Anyone who wants to win an election right now is a populist,” Phil Gardner, an adviser to centrist Democrats, told me

About Sanders, he said: “There is an increasing realization that his ideas have more currency and popularity than people might have thought back in 2016.” Sanders has shown few obvious signs of slowing down, either politically or physically
At each of his rallies in Maine, teleprompters that were in place for Jackson’s speech came down when it was Sanders’s turn to speak

His aides say that he checks in frequently with questions about logistics or policy. (Two of my own conversations with them were interrupted because Sanders was calling on the other line.) Sanders was also quicker than much younger politicians to recognize the public’s growing fears about AI, and he’s been one of the most aggressive leaders on the left in demanding more regulation of the industry and a moratorium on new data centers

Democrats are begging not only for his presence in key states and districts, but for his financial help as well: He’s raised millions of dollars for candidates during this election, and last week he gave $1 million to boost Abdul El-Sayed’s U.S
Senate candidacy in Michigan. [ Read: The only thing capable of uniting Bernie and Bannon ] Unlike most politicians, Sanders avoids talking much about himself
During his Maine speeches, he made only glancing references to his growing influence
At one point, he noted that he’s been talking about oligarchy for a number of years. “Before I started talking about it, people would say, What the hell is an oligarch? ” he told the crowd in Bangor

Then he added, to a loud cheer: “People know what oligarchy is today.” I met Sanders after the speech, and when I asked him to explain his widening appeal, he initially shrugged as if to dismiss the question

But he could not completely hide his satisfaction with the sense that after he spent decades on the fringes of political debates, the country was moving in his direction. “I think the American people are undergoing a massive transformation in their views,” Sanders told me. “So maybe Bernie Sanders has not been all that crazy over the years.” S anders has always had a complicated relationship with the Democratic Party

He sought its presidential nomination twice, but he still likes to remind voters that he has run for election to the Senate as an independent. (Along with the Senate’s other independent, Maine’s Angus King, he caucuses with the Democrats.) Despite that distinction, he began his remarks in Maine by urging voters to set aside every consideration but party label when they cast their ballot. “If you want to hold Donald Trump and his disastrous policies accountable,” Sanders said, “the only way we do that is by electing a Democratic Senate.” The pitch was clearly aimed at the many independents and Democrats who have supported Senator Susan Collins, a moderate Republican, in previous years. [ Read: Maine has changed

Susan Collins hasn’t. ] At the same time, Sanders also heaped plenty of criticism on Democrats, accusing them of deferring to corporate donors and ignoring the needs of the working class. “The Democratic Party itself is significantly responsible for the rise of Trumpism,” Sanders told me

He made clear that he hoped that the election of a slate of progressive Senate candidates—which includes Jackson, El-Sayed, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and Angie Nixon in Florida—would force the party to pursue policies it has previously deemed too radical
All four of these candidates have also called for replacing Chuck Schumer as the Democrats’ Senate leader
Sanders is not going that far yet, but he told me that he would support a leader “who’s going to fight for Medicare for All”—a position that Schumer has yet to embrace
Sanders, too, could have more say in shaping party policy: He’s in line to become chair of the Senate’s powerful Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions if Democrats win the majority
One reason Sanders is so much busier this fall is that so many of the candidates running in big races have him at least partially to thank for their nomination
Sanders endorsed more than 80 candidates for federal, state, and local offices this year—a higher total, his aides told me, than he has backed in the past
By their count, nearly 75 percent of them won their primary
He had a few misfires; most notably, Sanders was an early endorser of Graham Platner’s Senate candidacy in Maine and stood by him through a series of controversies

Sanders joined Democrats in abandoning Platner after he was accused of sexual assault, an accusation which he denied. (“Let’s not get into Platner,” Sanders told me when I brought him up.) Plenty of candidates have sought Sanders’s endorsement without getting it

title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
excerpt: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence
body: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence
Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers
Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover
The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look
A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how
That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business
The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing
The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth
Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant
Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful
For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record
They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made
Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated
When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor
More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows
But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity
Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products
When intelligence participates in action Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world
By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor
Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action
Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions
Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station
Vision can help the system assess a part’s position
A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement
Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits
The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately
The same principle applies to quality operations
When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers
The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%
The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in
This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential
Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment
Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment
Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment
That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment
Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline
Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions
People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state
Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone
More capable machines, more capable people Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools

title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
excerpt: Solid-state transformers do more with less: By swapping bulky steel cores for advanced semiconductors, solid-state versions can be one-tenth the size of convent
body: Solid-state transformers do more with less: By swapping bulky steel cores for advanced semiconductors, solid-state versions can be one-tenth the size of conventional transformers while absorbing the jobs of multiple devices—and losing half as much energy in the process

Data centers are the proving ground: Companies like Heron Power, which raised $140 million earlier this year, are targeting data centers first, where voltage requirements are lower and the money is flowing—with a California factory set to hit full production by 2029

High-voltage transmission remains the hard part: Solid-state transformers still can't handle the hundreds of thousands of volts needed for long-distance power lines, meaning the technology's biggest test—and biggest opportunity—is still ahead. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147684" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid
The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply

And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.  As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers
New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure
Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits

Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.  These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission
But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid
The grid’s backbone Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat
How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost
So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.  Consider, for example, your local solar plant
For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant

Enter transformers.  In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines
Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer
Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood

If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home
Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire
The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel

Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.  The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down
When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core
That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage
This process is called magnetic induction
Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University
In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them
That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says
A solid option Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers
While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current

Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.  From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage

Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer
Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC
Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job
But solid-state transformers can do much more

They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system
In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site
The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says
The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in
An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says

title: How religion collided with race and politics in Brazil’s presidential election

<title>How religion collided with race and politics in Brazil’s presidential election</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768433/original/file-20261027-52-3kiu9g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3239%2C2159&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Brazilian Christians pray during a service at the Assembly of God Victory in Christ evangelical church in Rio de Janeiro on Aug. 27, 2025.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BrazilEvangelicals/6b6a7a505437405f8aad497e9d351f60/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=brazil%20pray&amp;currentItemNo=1&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Silvia Izquierdo</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Since Brazil’s runoff elections, most attention has been focused on President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise upset.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/brazilians-head-polls-high-stakes-polarized-election-2026-10-04/">The first round of voting</a> gave a narrow lead to challenger Flávio Bolsonaro – son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is now serving <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/brazils-bolsonaro-sentenced-27-years-after-landmark-coup-plot-conviction-2025-09-12/">a 27-year sentence</a> for efforts to overturn the 2022 election. In <a href="https://apnews.com/article/brazil-election-lula-bolsonaro-runoff-vote-president-e2c9fe8fc4aa3e3675b9a8ec15405d93">a Oct. 25, 2026, comeback</a>, however, <a href="https://resultados.tse.jus.br/oficial/app/index.html#/eleicao/6258/uf/br/cargo/1/vis/nominal/resultados">Lula won nearly 52% of votes</a>, compared with the younger Bolsonaro’s 48%. </p>

<p>Yet the close results still highlight the country’s deep polarization, <a href="https://theconversation.com/faith-rhetoric-and-the-ballot-box-how-religion-has-shaped-brazils-current-presidential-election-293495">including religious divides</a>, which have played <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009275088">an increasingly important</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108699655">role in its politics</a>. According to <a href="https://arte.folha.uol.com.br/poder/eleicoes/2026/pesquisa-eleitoral/datafolha/?turno=segundo-turno&amp;local=brasil&amp;cargo=presidente&amp;pesquisa=intencao-de-voto-estimulada-votos-validos&amp;cenarios=cenario-a&amp;recorte=relig2&amp;subgrupo=evangelica">polls before the election</a>, Catholics were <a href="https://www.bbc.com/portuguese/articles/cmx2z70jq94wo">more likely to support Lula</a>, while evangelicals staunchly backed Bolsonaro.</p>

<p>But Brazil’s evangelicals have diverse beliefs and identities. As <a href="https://charleston.edu/political-science/faculty/thomas-john.php">a political scientist who studies Latin America</a>, I believe the full picture of how faith shapes the country’s politics is more complicated – especially when it comes to race.</p>

<h2>Changes in Christianity</h2>

<p>According to the <a href="https://www.ibge.gov.br/en/statistics/social/labor/22836-2022-census-3.html?edicao=43618&amp;t=resultados">latest national census</a>, 57% of Brazilians are Catholic and 27% are evangelical. That is a stark shift from just 30 years ago, when 8 in 10 Brazilians <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/jun/06/brazil-catholics-evangelicals-religion-census">considered themselves Catholic</a> and 1 in 10 were evangelical.</p>

<p>Beyond Christianity, 1% of Brazilians <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/parallels/2013/09/16/216890587/brazilian-believers-of-hidden-religion-step-out-of-shadows">practice Candomblé</a> <a href="https://theworld.org/stories/2013/08/15/brazils-only-indigenous-religion-coming-its-own">or Umbanda</a>, which draw on African religions. Two percent follow Spiritism, a movement that <a href="https://berkleycenter.georgetown.edu/posts/brazil-s-invisible-spirits">took root in Brazil</a> around the turn of the 20th century. Four percent belong to other religions, and 9% have no religious affiliation.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several women in long white skirts and T-shirts stand in sand at the edge of the ocean." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768439/original/file-20261027-62-px5w69.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Devotees pray during an Umbanda religious ceremony at Urca beach in Rio de Janeiro on Dec. 30, 2023.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BrazilUmbandaEndofYear/78b48014a66a474396e57c8ecef1fc55/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=brazil%20pray&amp;currentItemNo=53&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Bruna Prado</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>One measure of evangelicals’ growing influence is political. Almost 1 in 5 members of Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, <a href="https://religiaoepoder.org.br/artigo/pesquisa-do-iser-levanta-identidade-religiosa-dos-deputados-e-deputadas-federais-diplomados">identify as “evangelical.”</a></p>

<p>Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle, <a href="https://fox40.com/news/international/ap-international/ap-bolsonaro-campaign-to-evangelicals-brazils-soul-at-stake/">helped cement his support among many evangelicals</a> ahead of his 2018 election victory. His slogan of “God, country, family and freedom” won <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/e7a47196-1817-11ea-9ee4-11f260415385?syn-25a6b1a6=1">endorsements from key clergy</a>. As Flávio, his son, ran in the 2026 election, he also talked about religion, such as declaring that <a href="https://cbn.globo.com/coberturas/eleicoes-2026/noticia/2026/09/29/flavio-bolsonaro-diz-que-promessa-de-declarar-que-o-brasil-e-do-senhor-jesus-cristo-era-simbolica.ghtml">Brazil belongs “to the Lord Jesus Christ</a>.” </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman in a white shirt, whose eyes are closed, holds her hands up in prayer as she stands amid many other people." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768534/original/file-20261027-63-u3e4cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Brazil’s former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro prays for her husband, Jair Bolsonaro, at an evangelical church on the outskirts of Brasilia, Brazil, on July 24, 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BrazilBolsonaro/25697baae43843c1b1e81d7ca06c04d4/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=brazil%20pray&amp;currentItemNo=7&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Eraldo Peres</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But not all evangelicals are the same. Latin Americans often <a href="https://theconversation.com/religion-is-shaping-brazils-presidential-election-but-its-evangelicals-arent-the-same-as-americas-190509">consider anything Christian but not Catholic to be “evangelical.”</a> One wing of Protestant churches in Brazil is decidedly conservative and shares characteristics with evangelical churches in the United States. However, the category also includes denominations such as Methodists, Lutherans and Presbyterians. </p>

<p>Then there are Pentecostal groups like the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God and The Assembly of God, <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/figure/The-largest-Protestant-and-Pentecostal-Churches-in-Brazil-2010-Census_tbl1_267453543">Brazil’s largest non-Catholic denomination</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://iser.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Dados-iniciais-Pesquisa-Religiao-e-Vida-Publica-no-Brasil.pdf">Survey data from ISER</a>, a Brazilian think tank <a href="https://iser.org.br/en/religiaoevidapublicanobrasil/">focused on religion</a>, shows that members of Pentecostal and evangelical churches are more likely to reject Lula’s Workers’ Party than any another faith group, while practitioners of African-rooted religions are more likely to reject Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party than any other group.</p>

<h2>Religion and race</h2>

<p>Surveys <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781316888742">and research</a> also show <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-39904-6">clear political trends around race</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009472401">contrary to</a> <a href="https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_WYFFbVYEzvkC/page/n9/mode/2up">long-standing beliefs</a> among many Brazilians that race does not matter in their society.</p>

<p>Forty-five percent of Brazilians <a href="https://www.ibge.gov.br/en/statistics/social/labor/22836-2022-census-3.html?edicao=38732&amp;t=destaques">identify as Pardo, or “Brown,”</a> referring to people with multiracial ancestry. Forty-three percent identify as white, and 10% as Black. Around 0.6% are Indigenous, and 0.4% are East Asian.</p>

<p>Black Brazilians are <a href="https://arte.folha.uol.com.br/poder/eleicoes/2026/pesquisa-eleitoral/datafolha/?turno=segundo-turno&amp;local=brasil&amp;cargo=presidente&amp;pesquisa=intencao-de-voto-estimulada-votos-validos&amp;cenarios=cenario-a&amp;recorte=relig2&amp;subgrupo=catolica">more likely to support Lula</a>, while those identifying as white tend to support Bolsonaro, and people identifying as Brown are evenly divided.</p>

<p>Examining the intersection of religion and race is also important to understanding Brazil’s diversity. About half of Black Brazilians are Catholic, and <a href="https://biblioteca.ibge.gov.br/visualizacao/livros/liv102182.pdf">nearly 1 in 3 are evangelical</a>; in fact, <a href="https://books.google.com/books/about/A_religi%C3%A3o_mais_negra_do_Brasil.html?hl=pt-PT&amp;id=Nc2X1ygrE4MC">within Pentecostal and evangelical churches</a>, a majority are of African descent.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People standing as they sing or pray in a room with white walls and rows of chairs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768556/original/file-20261027-63-nopwxp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Brazilian Christians pray during a service at the Assembly of God Victory in Christ evangelical church in Rio de Janeiro on Aug. 27, 2025.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BrazilEvangelicals/bfe8913439744d74a1b3e7aeb20cf19e/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=brazil%20pray&amp;currentItemNo=4&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Silvia Izquierdo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Independent Black Christian denominations did not emerge in Brazil the way they did in the U.S.; those churches’ creation was, in part, a result of segregation. However, Black groups within religious organizations have long been <a href="https://mnebrasil.org/">involved in activism</a> to <a href="https://www.metodista.org.br/combate-ao-racismo-cmi/">address racism</a> <a href="https://www.cnbb.org.br/afro_brasileira/">and Black communities’ concerns</a>. Despite these efforts, leadership in both Catholic and evangelical circles has remained largely white.</p>

<p>During the late 2010s, a new generation of activists took the helm, concerned about <a href="https://religionnews.com/2019/04/25/practitioners-of-afro-brazilian-religions-fear-increasing-intolerance-under-bolsonaro/">intolerance toward Afro-Brazilian religions</a> and <a href="https://therevealer.org/the-solution-is-jesus-christian-nationalism-from-brazil-to-the-united-states/">growing Christian nationalism</a>, and some started to more vocally criticize the Bolsonaro administration. During the 2022 election, 14 evangelical organizations created a “<a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/CkQwD2sLBHo/?img_index=2">Brazilian Black Protestant Manifesto</a>” calling for the government to not favor any one religion, policies to address police violence against Black youth, women’s rights and other issues.</p>

<p>In 2025, political scientist <a href="https://www.nccu.edu/cash/political-science/dan-blue-endowed-chair">Gladys Mitchell-Walthour</a> and I attended <a href="https://mnebrasil.org/conferenciaenegrecer2025">the Enegrecer Conference</a> in São Paulo, which brought together 400 Afro-Brazilian evangelical laity and clergy calling for racial justice and progress in reducing socioeconomic inequality. A key point was rapprochement with Candomblé and Umbanda, <a href="https://theworld.org/stories/2022/07/29/afro-brazilian-religious-groups-are-under-attack">whose places of worship are often vandalized and damaged</a>. Ivanir dos Santos, a priest or “babalawo” in the Candomblé tradition, blessed the closing service. </p>

<h2>2026 election</h2>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in a white T-shirt and shorts kneels on the street in prayer, with a praying woman standing near him." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768566/original/file-20261027-62-2qo1pj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro pray in Brasilia after he lost the runoff election on Oct. 25, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/BrazilElection/219dd5b1d01a42d7b2d7e563dc3909bd/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=brazil&amp;currentItemNo=20&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Bruna Prado</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Throughout the current Brazilian election cycle, religion has become a polarizing force in its own right. For example, on Instagram, one will see posts like “Real Christians don’t vote for Lula,” or “I’m Christian, and I support Lula.”</p>

<p>Evangelical support for Jair Bolsonaro has been a prominent feature of all recent elections. But this time, it was less unusual to see evangelicals publicly support the left – many of them Preto or Pardo. </p>

<p>“<a href="https://pt.org.br/caravana-cristaos-pela-democracia-finaliza-em-salvador-com-grande-caminhada/">Christians for Democracy</a>,” for example, a group affiliated with Lula’s party, brought together prominent Black evangelicals and Catholics on panels and held prayer rallies. The group’s Instagram page <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/De8XsbvtNCo/">highlighted prominent leaders of Lula’s campaign</a> who are evangelical Christians, including former Environment Minister Mariana Silva, pastor and legislator Henrique Vieira, Attorney General Jorge Mesias, legislator and former Rio de Janeiro Gov. Benedita da Silva, and André Janones. Janones, a legislator from one of Brazil’s most populous states, was <a href="https://english.elpais.com/technology/2026-10-27/andre-janones-the-whatsapp-general-who-turned-the-brazil-election-around-for-lula.html">the head of “Lula’s Army,”</a> the 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was pivotal in Lula’s victory.</p>

<p>Lula’s victory is just one more example of how race intersects all facets of Brazilian society, including religion. I believe these durable divisions will mark Brazil’s political and religious landscape for the foreseeable future.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294761/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>John Thomas III is affiliated with the African Methodist Episcopal Church. </span></em></p></content>
