<title>Earwax is both slippery and sticky – this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766829/original/file-20261016-50-wq8tun.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=193%2C472%2C4381%2C2920&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Scientists watched as ants encountered earwax with various properties.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Candler Hobbs and David Hu</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects?</p>

<p>It’s earwax. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="earwax magnified" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=195&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=195&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=195&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=245&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=245&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766849/original/file-20261017-50-8wfmza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=245&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Sheep earwax at various levels of magnification. The matte surface is due to overlapping skin cells; the cracks between help absorb water.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">David Ancalle and David Hu</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/roman-tweezers-and-metal-q-tip-found-england-180973777/">picks and spoons to remove earwax</a> have been found <a href="https://historicjamestowne.org/collections/artifacts/ear-picker/">in archaeological sites worldwide</a>.</p>

<p>Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: <a href="https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/3-reasons-to-leave-earwax-alone-2017051711718">Don’t do it</a>. The general medical belief is that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0194599816680327">ears are self-cleaning</a>, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-earwax-170857">earwax brings benefits</a> such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.</p>

<p>Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/lio2.1228">fifth of the American population</a>, leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.</p>

<p>Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.</p>

<p>While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?</p>

<p>To answer this question, my Ph.D. student <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=GrNeeK4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">David Ancalle</a> led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=U9NeaxUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Yuhang Hu</a> and her student <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=hgPzCfsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">Donjing He</a>, experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/d6sm00737f">Our research</a>, published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.</p>

<h2>Watching ants encounter earwax</h2>

<p>To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.</p>

<p>Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1288/00005537-199003000-00012">grain of rice’s worth of earwax</a> in each ear. Due to a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/ng1733">mutation in a single gene</a>, East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4HZCPTiyAVY">wet, squishy earwax</a>.</p>

<p>To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.093021">ants have spikes on their feet</a>, like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/icb/42.6.1100">ants unfurl wet suction cups</a>, which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.</p>

<p>Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/RVFtQj39F2I?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Rough earwax was a challenge to climb, but feasible for the ants.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/2CPVSY2jtSg?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A smooth earwax coating made it impossible for ants to scale this microscope slide.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet. </p>

<p>We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Greatly magnified image of ant with yellow circles highlighting bits of stuck debris." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=589&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=589&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=589&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=740&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=740&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766846/original/file-20261017-50-2i5552.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=740&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Bits of earwax stick to the ant’s body.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">David Ancalle and David Hu</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning. </p>

<h2>Figuring out earwax’s physical properties</h2>

<p>The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.</p>

<p>When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nN_27GRfLcE?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Time-lapse video (one fifth actual speed) of earwax absorbing a 1.0 µL droplet of water.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-3190/ac91b9">prevent insects from climbing</a>.</p>

<p>From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.</p>

<p>The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as <a href="https://theconversation.com/swimmers-ear-doesnt-just-affect-swimmers-two-ear-doctors-explain-what-you-need-to-know-about-this-painful-condition-189213">swimmer’s ear</a>.</p>

<p>Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1128/aac.18.4.638">earwax kills bacteria</a>, but other studies find that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/qjmed/hch082">earwax harbors bacteria</a>.</p>

<p>Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022215100062800">epithelial migration</a> – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.</p>

<p>Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk <a href="https://doi.org/10.18196/mmjkk.v21i1.9576">or chew</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apergo.2023.104195">your ear canal deforms</a>, and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9wmSCV3p7ks?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Artificial earwax, with physical properties that mimicked the real thing, was hard for ants to traverse.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As a test of our concept, a member of our team, chemical engineer Rafeen Rahaman, designed <a href="https://biochemazone.com/product/artificial-cerumen-synthetic-earwax-bz171/">an artificial earwax</a> based on the physical structure rather than the chemistry of the earwax. Ants struggled when they touched it, just like when they interacted with natural earwax.</p>

<p>The cost of harvesting natural earwax and our recipe for artificial earwax are not cheap. We don’t foresee our methods replacing insect repellents produced at large scale. But perhaps the concept might inspire new ways to prevent earwax from coating our earbuds or lead to the manufacture of insect control methods using safe formulations.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293324/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765729/original/file-20261013-50-pcklkk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6566%2C4377&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A new survey will evaluate school library services in Michigan. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/librarian-assisting-elementary-student-royalty-free-image/2192145482?phrase=school%20librarians&amp;adppopup=true">Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.mischooldata.org/michigans-education-staff/">Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools</a> report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian. </p>

<p>Although Michigan strongly <a href="https://www.michigan.gov/mde/services/ed-serv/ed-cert/permits-placement/courses-that-can-be-taught/library-media">recommends that schools employ certified librarians</a>, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked <a href="https://libslide.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Section-405-School-Librarian-Employment-in-the-United-States-2025-C3-TK-1.pdf">46th in the student-to-librarian ratio</a>, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students. </p>

<p>The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/0161956X.2023.2160112">more isolated ones</a> like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, <a href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2022/7/18/23201078/cps-public-schools-librarians-misinformation-budget-cuts-pandemic-literacy-reading-books">exacerbating disparities in resources</a> for young people. </p>

<p>We are scholars in library and information sciences from <a href="https://sis.wayne.edu/news/a-spring-message-from-associate-dean-shannon-oltmann-69006">Wayne State University</a>, studying <a href="https://sis.wayne.edu/profile/id0481">information access and ethics</a> and <a href="https://sis.wayne.edu/profile/ak4901">equity in education and school libraries</a>. Currently, we are <a href="https://sis.wayne.edu/mi-school-census-2026">conducting a statewide campaign</a> to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more. </p>

<p>Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Shelves filled with books" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=337&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=337&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=337&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765730/original/file-20261013-50-kzoj0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools have a trained librarian.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=school%20librarian%20united%20states&amp;mediaType=photo">Harkim Wright Sr./AP</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Catalysts for student achievement</h2>

<p>A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide.</p>

<p>School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete <a href="https://sis.wayne.edu/school-library-media-specialist/required">advanced education</a>. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook.</p>

<p>Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/01930826.2020.1820278">higher student achievement</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/01930826.2020.1820278">improved student literacy</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/04250494.2018.1558030">especially for struggling readers</a>. They can instill <a href="https://www.proquest.com/docview/3291879165/AA63469378F64B65PQ/26?sourcetype=Scholarly%20Journals">a love</a> of <a href="https://scottishlibraries.org/vibrant-libraries-thriving-schools/">reading</a> and teach <a href="https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1096706.pdf">technological skills</a>, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence. </p>

<p>At our <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lxRPc5Mm1JU">Michigan School Census symposium</a> held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year. </p>

<p>At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school. </p>

<h2>Students’ information worlds</h2>

<p>Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI. </p>

<p>AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, <a href="https://www.turing.ac.uk/blog/what-are-deepfakes-and-how-can-we-detect-them">harming their reputations and undermining trust</a> in what people see online. </p>

<p>Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00304-3">even elementary school students</a> are learning about it. </p>

<h2>Building information literacy</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.naesp.org/resource/6-foundational-skills-librarians-can-help-cultivate/">Information literacy</a> means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice.</p>

<p>For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts?</p>

<p>The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence.</p>

<p>Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication. </p>

<h2>Becoming savvy digital citizens</h2>

<p>Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another. </p>

<p>Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video.</p>

<p>Recent <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/07380569.2026.2629965">research</a> emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments. </p>

<p>Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.imls.gov/grants/awarded/re-246399-ols-20">Project Restoring Urban School Libraries</a> helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information.</p>

<p>Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience.</p>

<h2>Fighting for recognition</h2>

<p>Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/01930826.2021.1924532">may complete their training</a> without learning how to work with a school librarian. </p>

<p>In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lxRPc5Mm1JU&amp;t=2880s">an instructional coach</a>.” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits.</p>

<p>School library jobs remain vulnerable to <a href="https://journals.library.ualberta.ca/slw/index.php/iasl/article/view/8554">budget cuts</a>, and <a href="https://bridgemi.com/talent-education/michigan-scrambles-improve-literacy-school-librarians-are-losing-their-jobs/">the number of school librarians</a> across the state has been decreasing since 2010. </p>

<p>To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our <a href="https://sage-marzipan-cfdb0b.netlify.app/">public response map</a> tracks participation across districts.</p>

<p>Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding.</p>

<p>Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on.</p>

body: A new survey will evaluate school library services in Michigan
Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian
Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians , the state does not require them
In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio , with one school librarian for every 2,760 students

The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people
We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University , studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries
Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more
Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it
Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens
Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools have a trained librarian
Harkim Wright Sr./AP Catalysts for student achievement A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf
A room full of books can look like a school library

But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide
School librarians bring those services to life
Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education
They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook

Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy , especially for struggling readers
They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills , which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence
At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like
Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed
He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year
At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers
A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school
Students’ information worlds Access to information is only a start
Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI
AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online
Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too
Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first
Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source
AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it
Building information literacy Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information
School librarians turn those skills into practice
For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record
Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts? The same habits apply to AI
Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer
A confident response still needs evidence

Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends
Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information
They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication
Becoming savvy digital citizens Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill

<title>We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767391/original/file-20261021-60-34ok4n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Ohio ranks No. 4 in the U.S. in terms of how many data centers it has, including this one in Springfield.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-aerial-view-of-the-5c-data-centers-cmh01-on-october-18-news-photo/2300875306?phrase=data%20centers&amp;adppopup=true">Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Data centers <a href="https://www.cushmanwakefield.com/en/united-states/insights/data-center-development-cost-guide">require enormous investments</a>: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to <a href="https://hamminstitute.org/site-files/documents/data_center_workforce.pdf">employ no more than a few dozen people</a> in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-better-off-cities-and-towns-see-more-benefits-from-data-centers-than-rural-regions-286750">asking what they will get in return</a>.</p>

<p>Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/709772/americans-oppose-data-centers-area.aspx">growing opposition to their construction</a>, <a href="https://farmoffice.osu.edu/blog/mon-04062026-1124am/data-center-controversies-continue-ohio">from Ohio</a> <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/10/14/texas-data-centers-water-use-penalties-enforcement/">to Texas</a>. That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/26/business/economy/ai-data-centers-construction-local-opposition.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com">US$156 billion in proposed data center projects</a> in 2025 alone.</p>

<p>We are <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=xAOSK2QAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">professors who study real estate</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=bf9yjsQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">urban economics</a>, including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?</p>

<p>To find out, <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7467778">we teamed up with four colleagues</a> to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.</p>



<h2>How data centers create local jobs</h2>

<p>Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.</p>

<p>First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.</p>

<p>Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.</p>

<p>Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A technician works inside a data center." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767394/original/file-20261021-50-qexcr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Data centers, like this one run by Amazon Web Services in New Carlisle, Ind., employ few people.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-this-handout-provided-by-amazon-a-technician-works-at-an-news-photo/2249021916?phrase=data%20center%20jobs&amp;adppopup=true">Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Tracking data centers and jobs</h2>

<p>We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.</p>

<p>Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.</p>

<p>To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.</p>

<h2>Jobs appear, but not immediately</h2>

<p>During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.</p>

<p>Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs.</p>

<p>Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A vast data center under construction transforms the landscape." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=493&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=493&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=493&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=620&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=620&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767392/original/file-20261021-50-sfelub.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=620&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Stargate Oracle AI data center, which is under construction in Abilene, Texas, will span roughly 4 million square feet and will be operated by Oracle for OpenAI.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-sections-of-the-stargate-oracle-ai-data-news-photo/2292234929?phrase=data%20centers%20texas&amp;adppopup=true">Brandon Bell/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Jobs are not where you might expect</h2>

<p>The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.</p>

<p>Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.</p>

<p>By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.</p>

<p>We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.</p>

<h2>Jobs are only one side of the equation</h2>

<p>Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the <a href="https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/monthly-spending-data-center-us">current wave of massive facilities were built</a> to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.</p>

<p>We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/16/climate/ai-environmental-impact-energy-water-noise-explainer">electricity and water, can generate noise</a> and may receive <a href="https://www.cbpp.org/blog/states-began-scaling-back-expensive-subsidies-for-data-centers-in-this-years-legislative">substantial tax breaks</a> from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.</p>

<p>Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293872/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad
url:
<title>Leave home with a plan: What to pack in your medical kit and when to seek care for symptoms abroad</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764692/original/file-20261007-50-q6nnmv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=547%2C0%2C5913%2C3942&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">When traveling abroad, asking your doctor ahead of time about treatments for minor ailments can help keep your trip on track.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-passenger-in-airplane-seat-holding-stomach-royalty-free-image/2280116851?phrase=travel%20abroad%20health&amp;adppopup=true">Nansan Houn/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When people prepare to see a doctor before an international trip, vaccines usually dominate the conversation.</p>

<p>And while vaccines are important, many of the health problems most likely to derail a trip cannot be prevented with a vaccine: Diarrhea, respiratory infections, motion sickness and flare-ups of existing medical conditions are all common – and none of them can be headed off with a shot.</p>

<p>The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/post-travel-evaluation/post-travel-evaluation-of-the-ill-traveler.html">between 43% and 79% of travelers</a> to low- and middle-income countries become ill during or after their trip, although most of those illnesses are mild.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Zykl2poAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">infectious diseases physician</a> who specializes in travel and tropical medicine, I counsel many patients before they leave the country and care for them when they come home sick.</p>

<p>A good pretravel visit to the doctor should end with more than a list of shots. You should know which illnesses you could encounter on your itinerary, which symptoms you can reasonably handle yourself, which medicines to carry and how to use them, and which warning signs mean it is time to find a doctor. </p>

<h2>Serious illnesses</h2>

<p>Infectious disease risks abroad are constantly shifting. A good healthcare provider who specializes in travel and geographic medicine keeps up with these developments so that the advice you get reflects what is happening now, not last year.</p>

<p>Since early 2025, South America has seen new yellow fever outbreaks that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lana.2026.101431">redrew long-standing risk maps</a> and an unusual <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2026.9419">hantavirus cluster that spread</a> from <a href="https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON599">person to person aboard a cruise ship</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/dengue-carrying-mosquitoes-expand-their-reach-into-new-territories-including-florida-291837">Cases of dengue fever</a> worldwide roughly <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijid.2025.107940">doubled in a single year</a>, and another tropical disease – <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chikungunya">chikungunya</a> – also flared in new places, including the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanmic.2025.101261">largest outbreak ever recorded in China</a>. Fiji declared a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/26/g-s1-144667/hiv-crystal-meth-epidemic-fiji">fast-growing HIV outbreak</a>. And common respiratory viruses, from influenza to COVID-19, continue to circulate all over the world.</p>

<p>In my own clinical research with colleagues, we have seen travelers who returned to the U.S. with serious – and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/jtm/taz008">occasionally fatal</a> – infections, such as <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/malaria/symptoms-causes/syc-20351184">malaria</a> and <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/hepatitis.html">hepatitis</a>, often <a href="https://doi.org/10.4269/ajtmh.18-0010">after dangerous delays</a> in recognizing what was wrong.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<h2>Let your itinerary guide the conversation</h2>

<p>Travel health advice is not one-size-fits-all. A week at a Caribbean resort, a safari in East Africa and a month trekking in Nepal carry very different risks.</p>

<p>Even the likely cause of a fever changes with the destination. Dengue is a leading concern after travel in much of Latin America and Asia, while malaria is especially important in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and <a href="https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/typhoid-and-paratyphoid">typhoid and paratyphoid fever</a> loom largest in South Asia. </p>

<p>What you do matters, too – freshwater swimming, visiting caves, animal contact, hiking and staying in remote areas each <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/post-travel-evaluation/post-travel-evaluation-of-the-ill-traveler.html">add their own hazards</a>.</p>

<p>So bring your actual itinerary to the appointment. Tell your doctor not just which countries you’ll visit, but whether you’ll be in cities or the countryside, what you plan to do, how high you’ll go, how long you’ll stay and how easily you could reach a reliable hospital.</p>

<h2>Illnesses you can safely treat yourself</h2>

<p>For minor illnesses, you can plan to treat yourself. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/travelers-diarrhea.html">Travelers’ diarrhea</a> is the best example of such an illness. Depending on the destination and season, it affects an estimated 10% to 40% of travelers during the first two weeks of a trip. Most cases clear up on their own within a few days, but having a plan makes a real difference.</p>

<p>Ask your doctor what to do if diarrhea develops. Oral rehydration salts help replace fluids when losses are heavy. <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements/loperamide-oral-route/description/drg-20064573">Loperamide</a>, an over-the-counter antidiarrheal, can reduce how often and how urgently you need a bathroom, but it should not be used on its own when diarrhea comes with a fever or blood in the stool. Depending on your destination and medical history, your doctor may also give you an antibiotic to carry and use only for moderate or severe diarrhea.</p>

<p>When it comes to treatments you’ll be administering yourself, it’s as important to ask your doctor when to use each medicine as it is to have the drugs on hand. Antibiotics have side effects, can leave you carrying drug-resistant bacteria and contribute to <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/antimicrobial-resistance">antibiotic resistance worldwide</a> – so they are best saved for the episodes that truly need them.</p>

<p>The same logic applies to other predictable problems. Someone <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/travel-air-sea/motion-sickness.html">prone to seasickness</a> on a planned boat trip might discuss <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements/meclizine-oral-route/description/drg-20075849">meclizine</a> or a <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements/scopolamine-transdermal-route/description/drg-20072848">scopolamine patch</a>. A traveler flying straight into a high-altitude city such as Cusco, Peru, or La Paz, Bolivia, might discuss acetazolamide, a prescription medicine that helps the body acclimatize and roughly <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/high-altitude-travel-and-altitude-illness.html">halves the risk of altitude sickness</a> during rapid ascents.</p>

<h2>Build a small medical kit – not a portable pharmacy</h2>

<p>A <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/travel-health-kits.html">basic travel health kit</a> keeps a small problem from becoming a big one. The contents depend on the traveler and the trip, but useful items include pain and fever medicine, bandages, antiseptic, <a href="https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-FCH-CAH-06.1">oral rehydration salts</a>, <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements/loperamide-oral-route/description/drg-20064573">loperamide</a>, antihistamine and anything prescribed specifically for the trip.</p>

<p>People with chronic conditions should <a href="https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/travel-abroad-with-medicine">pack enough of their regular medications</a> for the entire trip, plus extra in case of delays. Keep medicines in their original labeled containers, carry them in your hand luggage rather than checked bags, and consider bringing a copy of your prescriptions written with the drugs’ generic names.</p>

<p>Replacing a medication abroad can be harder than you expect. Drugs may have different names, formulations or availability in other countries, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/dangerous-counterfeit-drugs-are-putting-millions-of-us-consumers-at-risk-according-to-a-new-study-183585">counterfeit or low-quality medicines</a> remain a real problem in some places. Some medications that are routine in the U.S. are restricted or banned elsewhere. Insulin, injectable drugs, controlled substances and anything that needs refrigeration will require extra planning.</p>

<h2>Be skeptical of popular travel remedies</h2>

<p>Travel medicine is full of remedies with better reputations than evidence. Ginger is often recommended for motion sickness, but <a href="https://doi.org/10.1159/000138781">studies have produced mixed results</a>. Acupressure wristbands for motion sickness <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15018290/">do not outperform placebos</a>. And despite their popularity, <a href="https://theconversation.com/your-gut-microbes-can-be-anti-aging-scientists-are-uncovering-how-to-keep-your-microbiome-youthful-275380">probiotics</a> are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tmaid.2024.102703">not recommended for preventing travelers’ diarrhea</a>, as their efficacy is still unknown.</p>

<p>Coca leaves and coca tea are widely used for altitude symptoms in the Andes, but there is <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/complementary-and-integrative-health-approaches.html">no strong evidence</a> that they prevent altitude illness – and the same is true of garlic, ginkgo and vitamin E. “<a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/complementary-and-integrative-health-approaches.html">Natural” does not mean effective</a>, or even harmless, particularly when a <a href="https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/mixing-medications-and-dietary-supplements-can-endanger-your-health">supplement interacts with a prescription drug</a>.</p>

<h2>Ask about when to seek medical care</h2>

<p>Perhaps the most important part of any plan is recognizing when self-care is no longer appropriate.</p>

<p>Seek medical attention for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, difficulty breathing, confusion, severe abdominal pain or an illness that is rapidly getting worse. Bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with a significant fever calls for medical care rather than simply taking an antidiarrheal and carrying on with your trip.</p>

<p>At high altitudes, shortness of breath while resting, confusion, or difficulty walking a straight line are warning signs. Severe <a href="https://theconversation.com/altitude-sickness-is-typically-mild-but-can-sometimes-turn-very-serious-a-high-altitude-medicine-physician-explains-how-to-safely-prepare-222057">altitude illness</a> is treated by descending and getting medical care – another cup of coca tea is not an adequate substitute.</p>

<p>Fever after travel to an area where malaria is common deserves special attention. Malaria can turn deadly within hours, so get evaluated promptly and make sure the clinician knows where you have been. Some travel-related infections surface <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/post-travel-evaluation/post-travel-evaluation-of-the-ill-traveler.html">weeks or even months after you get home</a>, which is why your travel history stays relevant long after your suitcase is unpacked.</p>

<h2>Leave home with a plan</h2>

<p>I encourage travelers to make a medical contingency plan. Ask yourself: If my flight home were canceled and I had to stay abroad another week, would I have enough medication? If I developed diarrhea tomorrow, would I know what to take? If I spiked a fever, would I know when and where to seek care?</p>

<p>International travel will never be risk-free. But preparing for the problems most likely to happen can keep a manageable illness from becoming a medical emergency.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293602/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>How should AI be regulated? Follow the harm</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764295/original/file-20261006-106-e20ems.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C679%2C452&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">OpenAI CEO Sam Altman addresses AI risk at the U.N. Security Council on Sept. 23, 2026, two months after his company&#39;s latest model hacked into Hugging Face&#39;s systems. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/of-openai-sam-altman-speaks-during-a-united-nations-news-photo/2296796551">Alexi J. Rosenfeld via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As artificial intelligence technologies grow ever more powerful, so do the risks they pose and with them the urgency of regulating AI.</p>

<p>In July 2026, OpenAI’s advanced models <a href="https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/">hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s systems</a> during internal cybersecurity evaluations by communicating through unauthorized channels and working around safeguards developers had imposed on the models. In January 2026, Google and Character.ai, which makes a role-playing AI chatbot, agreed to <a href="https://people.com/teens-mom-settles-with-google-and-ai-company-after-claiming-his-suicide-was-fueled-by-love-of-chatbot-11881597">settle a wrongful death lawsuit</a> brought by Megan Garcia. Her 14-year-old son, who used the chatbot heavily, died by suicide. </p>

<p>As these and other cases show, AI harms can emerge across different technologies, organizations and contexts. As a legal scholar focused on <a href="https://scholar.google.com.au/citations?hl=en&amp;user=1jTquTsAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">AI and digital harms</a>, I study how to regulate AI.</p>

<p>Policymakers and industry commentators have tended to frame regulation as a trade-off between the risks of AI and the risks of regulating AI. In its <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf">2025 AI Action Plan</a>, the Trump administration called for removing “red tape and onerous regulation,” which it said hinders economic growth. The administration has also sought to limit conflicting state AI laws. </p>

<p>In contrast to the broad concerns about the costs of AI regulation, AI harms have largely been addressed through rules specific to particular technologies. The federal Take It Down Act, signed in 2025, for example, <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-the-take-it-down-act-tackles-nonconsensual-deepfake-porn-and-how-it-falls-short-255809">addresses nonconsensual intimate imagery</a>, including AI-generated deepfakes, as do <a href="https://www.citizen.org/article/tracker-intimate-deepfakes-state-legislation/">various state laws</a>. These approaches are crucial, but they don’t solve the problem by themselves.</p>

<p>The emerging patchwork of rules has yet to establish a regulatory architecture that connects protected interests, institutional obligations and individual rights across AI technologies. Protected interests are rights recognized by the law, such as property ownership and personal privacy. A <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-harm-is-often-behind-the-scenes-and-builds-over-time-a-legal-scholar-explains-how-the-law-can-adapt-to-respond-240080">harm-centered approach</a> would begin with those interests and use them to shape legal obligations that span relevant systems, organizations and people. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/FCXWgZjybm0?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Did an AI chatbot encourage 14-year-old Sewell Setzer to commit suicide?</span></figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>Types of harm</h2>

<p>A harm-centered approach starts by identifying the fundamental interests that AI systems can threaten. These overlapping interests include: </p>

<ul>
<li>Privacy: when AI systems improperly collect, process or disclose personal information.</li>
<li>Autonomy: when AI systems target a person’s vulnerabilities and manipulate their choices or encourage unhealthy dependence.</li>
<li>Equality: when AI systems discriminate or reinforce bias.</li>
<li>Safety: when AI systems cause physical, psychological or security harms.</li>
</ul>

<p>These examples are not exhaustive. Other interests may also be at stake as AI technologies evolve.</p>

<p>The same interest can be threatened by different technologies and different entities. A teenager’s safety can be harmed by the engagement mechanisms of a social media platform or by an AI companion designed to sustain an emotional relationship. </p>

<p>Designing regulations based on a concept of harm allows laws and principles to follow problems as the technology changes. And it helps <a href="https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4949052">determine obligations imposed on developers, deployers and other stakeholders</a> involved in AI. </p>

<p>For instance, AI developers could be required to conduct harm assessments throughout the development of AI systems, identifying reasonably foreseeable harms, documenting how they tested for them and explaining what mitigation measures they took. Companies or government agencies that deploy AI systems could also have duties to monitor harms after deployment. Serious or recurring harms could trigger obligations to report them to relevant regulators, affected individuals or the public, depending on the nature and severity of the harm.</p>

<p>A harm-centered framework could also recognize corresponding <a href="https://www.floridalawreview.com/article/168183-regulating-ai-harms">rights for people</a> affected by AI systems, including rights to notice and opportunities to seek redress where appropriate. These rights would arise from the same protected interests that justify obligations on companies. </p>

<p>The point is to build a regulatory architecture on the detection and reduction of harm across AI applications, developers and users. What matters most is whether and how AI-enabled design or operation contribute to harm.</p>

<h2>A common basis for law</h2>

<p>This mindset is followed in other areas of law. </p>

<p>Environmental law, for instance, has long regulated industries by focusing on their environmental effects rather than on technology alone. It requires regulated companies to monitor emissions and discharges, maintain records and report specified releases to <a href="https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/emergency-planning-and-community-right-know-act-epcra-and-federal-facilities">regulators</a>. Some reporting requirements also make information available to the public. Environmental review under the <a href="https://www.epa.gov/nepa">National Environmental Policy Act</a> requires federal agencies to assess environmental effects and provides opportunities for public participation. </p>

<p>AI governance could draw on this logic, determining who is responsible for assessment, monitoring, disclosure and mitigation based on types of harm.</p>

<p>A harm-based focus would not eliminate technology-specific rules. Some technologies create distinctive risks that justify targeted rules, such as disclosure requirements for AI-generated deepfakes or safeguards for AI systems used in high-stakes decisions. And focusing on harm does not mean regulating every conceivable risk of harm. </p>

<p>But I believe that harm should become the organizing principle of AI regulation. New AI systems will bring harms policymakers have not yet anticipated. The challenge is to build a framework for the harms we know, as well as the harms we do not yet know.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292350/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Her 14-year-old son, who used the chatbot heavily, died by suicide
As these and other cases show, AI harms can emerge across different technologies, organizations and contexts
As a legal scholar focused on AI and digital harms , I study how to regulate AI
Policymakers and industry commentators have tended to frame regulation as a trade-off between the risks of AI and the risks of regulating AI
In its 2025 AI Action Plan , the Trump administration called for removing “red tape and onerous regulation,” which it said hinders economic growth
The administration has also sought to limit conflicting state AI laws
In contrast to the broad concerns about the costs of AI regulation, AI harms have largely been addressed through rules specific to particular technologies
The federal Take It Down Act, signed in 2025, for example, addresses nonconsensual intimate imagery , including AI-generated deepfakes, as do various state laws
These approaches are crucial, but they don’t solve the problem by themselves
The emerging patchwork of rules has yet to establish a regulatory architecture that connects protected interests, institutional obligations and individual rights across AI technologies
Protected interests are rights recognized by the law, such as property ownership and personal privacy
A harm-centered approach would begin with those interests and use them to shape legal obligations that span relevant systems, organizations and people
Did an AI chatbot encourage 14-year-old Sewell Setzer to commit suicide? Types of harm A harm-centered approach starts by identifying the fundamental interests that AI systems can threaten
These overlapping interests include: Privacy: when AI systems improperly collect, process or disclose personal information
Autonomy: when AI systems target a person’s vulnerabilities and manipulate their choices or encourage unhealthy dependence
Equality: when AI systems discriminate or reinforce bias
Safety: when AI systems cause physical, psychological or security harms
Other interests may also be at stake as AI technologies evolve
The same interest can be threatened by different technologies and different entities
A teenager’s safety can be harmed by the engagement mechanisms of a social media platform or by an AI companion designed to sustain an emotional relationship
Designing regulations based on a concept of harm allows laws and principles to follow problems as the technology changes
And it helps determine obligations imposed on developers, deployers and other stakeholders involved in AI

For instance, AI developers could be required to conduct harm assessments throughout the development of AI systems, identifying reasonably foreseeable harms, documenting how they tested for them and explaining what mitigation measures they took
Companies or government agencies that deploy AI systems could also have duties to monitor harms after deployment
Serious or recurring harms could trigger obligations to report them to relevant regulators, affected individuals or the public, depending on the nature and severity of the harm
A harm-centered framework could also recognize corresponding rights for people affected by AI systems, including rights to notice and opportunities to seek redress where appropriate
These rights would arise from the same protected interests that justify obligations on companies
The point is to build a regulatory architecture on the detection and reduction of harm across AI applications, developers and users
What matters most is whether and how AI-enabled design or operation contribute to harm
A common basis for law This mindset is followed in other areas of law
Environmental law, for instance, has long regulated industries by focusing on their environmental effects rather than on technology alone
It requires regulated companies to monitor emissions and discharges, maintain records and report specified releases to regulators
Some reporting requirements also make information available to the public
Environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act requires federal agencies to assess environmental effects and provides opportunities for public participation
AI governance could draw on this logic, determining who is responsible for assessment, monitoring, disclosure and mitigation based on types of harm
