title: Why James Comey is getting charged again
excerpt: James Comey speaks onstage at an event in New York City on May 30, 2023. | Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newslett
body: James Comey speaks onstage at an event in New York City on May 30, 2023. | Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s revenge campaign is getting increasingly desperate.  What’s happening? On Monday, we learned that Trump’s Justice Department is criminally charging former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, in the latest installment of Trump’s ongoing efforts to prosecute his enemies
Unlike two previous instances, the charges are not in the form of an indictment

Instead, the DOJ filed a two-count criminal information, which allows prosecutors to lodge charges without getting a grand jury involved (but, crucially, does not allow the government to try Comey on those charges unless he waives his right to a grand jury).  What is Comey charged with? The charges allege that in October 2016, Comey unlawfully transmitted national security information about US email surveillance to a journalist

They were filed earlier this month on October 5, exactly 10 years after the alleged disclosure, after which point the statute of limitations would have expired.  Comey denies the charges, and said in a video posted Monday that the case “would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice.”  What’s the context? Comey, whom Trump fired as FBI director in 2017, has long been at the top of Trump’s second-term enemies list

He was indicted on scanty allegations of lying to Congress in September 2025, and again this spring for an alleged threat against Trump , in the form of a photo of seashells arranged to spell “86 47” (“86” is broadly understood to be service industry slang for rejecting or removing something or someone).  The first set of charges quickly fell flat after a judge found that the US attorney who brought them — former Trump lawyer Lindsey Halligan — was illegally appointed

Comey is still seeking to have the second set dismissed .  What’s the big picture? It’s unclear if this third set of charges will stick, though the Trump administration says it still plans to seek a grand jury indictment
But their existence underscores how dramatically Trump has succeeded in politicizing the Justice Department
And with that, it’s time to log off… How does creativity work? My colleagues at Vox’s Unexplainable podcast went looking for answers in a fascinating recent episode
You can hear all about what they found here
As always, thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Republicans are coming for your blue M&Ms
excerpt: A close-up image shows a bowl of blue M&M candies. | Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images If you were anything like me as a kid, trick-or-treating meant one, maybe two
body: A close-up image shows a bowl of blue M&M candies. | Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images If you were anything like me as a kid, trick-or-treating meant one, maybe two, pillowcases full of candy every Halloween.  And as fun as collecting all that candy could be, the real fun began when I got home and dumped my winnings onto my bedroom floor
I had some very specific rules: The usual suspects — think Smarties, Tootsie Rolls, and Dum Dums — went into one pile
Fun-size chocolates, like Snickers, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, and Baby Ruths, went into another
And then there was my prized pile: Skittles, Warheads, Starbursts, and Sour Patch Kids
Those were meant to be eaten slowly throughout November
The rest was fair game.  The ways we sort and eat our Halloween candy are decided by some very particular, personal rules
But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F

Kennedy Jr. would like to add another distinction: Which candies are made with artificial dyes? Kennedy’s ire for synthetic food dyes is years old, and they’ve become a major target of his Make America Healthy Again movement

Last year, he announced a plan to remove “petroleum-based synthetic dyes” from foods, arguing that companies “shouldn’t be feeding it to the rest of us.” That plan has become a multimillion-dollar problem for Mars, the maker of M&Ms, which promised customers last year that they would create an all-natural version of their tasty chocolatey treats

As the Wall Street Journal reported this summer, however, its latest offering is missing one of the most iconic colored M&Ms — the blue M&M.  M&Ms aren’t the only snack food in Kennedy’s crosshairs: He has called out Doritos, Cheez-Its, Cap’n Crunch, and gummy bears, saying their ingredients include “a lot of poisons.” On Fox News, he described what children eat as “food-like substances” and also said that “some of it was made in petroleum refineries.” In reality, the evidence is more complicated, because the Food and Drug Administration has long considered many of these approved synthetic dyes to be safe under its rules, while acknowledging that some children may be sensitive to them
Kennedy’s sweeping accusations go much further.  Still, pressure from Kennedy and those in the MAHA movement has led many companies to rethink the recipes of your favorite snacks

But producing those alternatives isn’t easy or cheap, as the story of the blue M&M illustrates.  Jesse Newman , a food reporter for the Wall Street Journal, went inside a Mars factory in Topeka, Kansas, to see the process for herself
She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about why blue is so difficult to produce naturally, and what changing a candy’s color actually accomplishes
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
The Secretary of Health and Human Services, RFK Jr., has some issues with the blue M&M
What, what exactly happened? How did it draw his attention?  He is not a fan of any sort of chemical
He’s really concerned about toxins in our food
And Blue 1, which is the food dye that makes blue M&Ms blue, is a synthetic chemical.  He really takes issue with artificial dyes
He believes that they cause hyperactivity in kids, some neurological challenges
He thinks artificial dyes are linked to cancer.  As a member of the Trump administration, he formally set out to get them removed, didn’t he?  Oh yeah
He’s been putting a lot of pressure on the industry to strip artificial dyes from all kinds of products
What do we know factually about artificial dyes? We hear that they’re bad for us
We hear that a lot of things are bad for us
Are artificial dyes really detrimental to our health?  The FDA for decades has said that there are nine artificial dyes approved for use in food

And they said that those artificial dyes are safe and have said so for years and years and years, as have other global bodies, so long as they’re used in accordance with some of the standards that the FDA laid out.  A California state agency has found that dyes are linked again to hyperactivity in children

And the FDA itself has said, ‘Okay, we think that these dyes are safe for the vast majority of kids, but some kids might be more sensitive to them than others.’ So I think the real issue is that it’s a chemical doing it
They don’t do anything except color food
There is no nutritional benefit that you are getting from these dyes
And so do we need them? Absolutely not.  I think one of the issues is that if you’re looking at the ways our food contributes to health problems, artificial dyes are probably pretty low on the list
You went inside a factory where they make M&Ms, and you looked at how they’re trying to make this happen
I went to this plant in Topeka, Kansas, to see how they were made
And it’s a massive industrial food plant, where they mix these colors and spray them onto these small chocolate orbs, which they refer to as lentils
The M&Ms move through the plant, and they arrive at these massive [machines] that they call pans, but they look like big tumble dryers
And the M&Ms just tumble around in these pans, and the color is sprayed on
It’s a very, very industrial process, millions of M&Ms a day
And the challenge that Mars has now is making that happen with a natural dye instead of an artificial one
What are the problems? They’ve been working on this for years
And they went with a product called spirulina, which is made from algae
But spirulina comes with a host of problems that they are now dealing with.  Blue 1, which is the artificial dye, arrives at the factories as a liquid

title: Benjamin Netanyahu’s day of reckoning is here
excerpt: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacts after filling out his ballot at a polling station in Jerusalem on October 27, 2026. | Yonatan Sindel/Getty Ima
body: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacts after filling out his ballot at a polling station in Jerusalem on October 27, 2026. | Yonatan Sindel/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Another day, another hugely consequential foreign election . (If you’re wondering why all the world seems to be voting now, there’s no conspiracy — it’s largely coincidence!)  Today we’re jetting off to Israel, where voters turned out in record numbers for what some analysts have called the most important legislative election in the country’s history
It’s an election that will determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stays in power — and could shape the future of Israeli democracy

These are, after all, the first national elections since the October 7, 2023, attacks, and they’re a referendum on everything that’s happened since: the devastating war in Gaza , the widening conflict across the Middle East, and Netanyahu’s attacks on independent watchdogs, foreign media, and his political opposition
Both Netanyahu and the opposition have depicted the election in existential terms
Campaign banners for Netanyahu’s Likud party warned Israelis that they could cast a vote for a right-wing party…or for Palestine
Opposition leaders, meanwhile, are framing the election as a fight to preserve Israeli democracy
Go a little deeper Some of you, I realize, may question whether Israel qualifies as a democracy at all, given its treatment of Palestinians

Listen: I appreciate the complexity here! That complexity is central to the stakes of this election.  Israeli democracy — whatever its asterisks — faces both an immediate threat and a more foundational problem
The immediate threat is, of course, Netanyahu and his more authoritarian impulses
A record seventh term would give him more time to weaken checks on his power
The foundational problem, meanwhile, concerns who gets a say in how Israel is governed

The state rules over Palestinians who cannot vote in its national elections, while its own Arab citizens — who make up one-fifth of the population — face well-documented discrimination in areas including housing, land use, and family reunification
That marginalization also shows up in politics
Both Netanyahu and several opposition leaders have vowed not to work with Israel’s Arab parties to form a governing coalition.  But that’s where this election could get interesting
Under Israel’s parliamentary system, Israelis essentially vote for a party, and parliamentary seats are allocated proportionally

Aligned parties then band together to try to form a coalition that can command the majority of parliamentary seats.  A Netanyahu coalition would likely include, for instance, a number of right-wing, nationalist and ultra-Orthodox parties, while an opposition coalition would likely include Jewish parties from the left, center, and center-right.  Either bloc could win enough seats today to govern without additional partners. (Polls closed at 4 pm ET, and we’ll have a fuller picture as the evening goes on.) But if the opposition falls short, it might need support from one or more of the Arab parties that some of its leading figures have lately sworn off.  Should no one form a governing coalition, Israelis may have to vote again

But more importantly, for our purposes, the debate over partnering with Arab parties goes back to that “ deeper foundational problem in Israeli democracy ,” as Vox’s Zack Beauchamp once put it.  As Zack argues, most Israeli Jews want to live in a democracy — but paradoxically, they want to live in a democracy that privileges some citizens over others

Netanyahu has tried to resolve that paradox by weakening Israel’s democratic institutions.  Today’s election and its aftermath could show whether there’s appetite in Israel for a very different, pro-democratic approach
Democracy is 2-0 this week ! We’ll soon see if it puts a third win on the board.  One link for later ➨ Treat your bot banker with care
Research shows that AI tools like ChatGPT dispense pretty good financial advice , on the whole
But you should still approach these tools with caution
Sharing specific financial information with a chatbot raises privacy concerns, and chatbots are not licensed or regulated the way human advisors or accountants are

Think of them as financially savvy friends: helpful…but fallible!   Before you go… Did you know …that a desire to please other people is one of the most common reasons people tell lies ? It’s more common than lying for both personal gain or pleasure
Today’s trivia: What’s the name of the lovable yellow dog in the comic strip Garfield? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the first predominantly white community in the US to vote in favor of school integration
That would be Teaneck, New Jersey, which in 1964 began bussing all of its sixth-grade students to a new central school building.

title: Is the “good” AI company actually making everything worse?
excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says his AI company can drive a “race to the top.” Where’s the evidence? | Finn Gomez/Getty Images We’re living through an AI-fueled
body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says his AI company can drive a “race to the top.” Where’s the evidence? | Finn Gomez/Getty Images We’re living through an AI-fueled “ Black October ,” and things are changing fast
Hackers are using AI to breach countless companies
AI tools have uncovered security flaws that could leave 70 percent of all websites vulnerable
Governments are scrambling to secure their sites
And because cyberhacks can hurt supply chains, some longtime AI watchers are going full prepper , stocking up on food, cash, and more
In the center of this story is Anthropic, one of the world’s leading AI companies, which was explicitly founded on the promise that it would be a “good guy” company in a world of dubious tech giants
Anthropic says all the latest developments are very serious

Its security chief wrote last week that things are “going to get a lot worse before they get better.” Two weeks ago the company warned that AI models could soon self-replicate on the internet-connected devices in your home, like smart fridges and robot vacuums

And its co-founder now says “ the singularity ” — when AI systems speed up technical progress in a way that’s hard for humans to comprehend — “is here.” You might think, given its view of the risks, that Anthropic would be pumping the brakes on its cutting-edge AI progress

Anthropic filed for a blockbuster initial public offering on Monday, chasing a valuation of $2 trillion even as it warns in the IPO filing that AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Every day, it is racing toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) , where AI models are smart enough to build the next, even smarter AI models by themselves.  How does Anthropic justify that? As its CEO, Dario Amodei, reminded the world last week, he built the company on one big bet: that instead of driving a race to the bottom, where companies skimp on safety in their rush to beat competitors in the market, Anthropic could actually catalyze a “race to the top.”  Why I wrote this story As I’ve watched Anthropic double down on its “race to the top” strategy, I’ve been uncomfortably reminded of another very risky gambit: Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto fraud of 2022
There are important differences between the two; this is not a perfect parallel
But both involve a tiny handful of figures, strongly influenced by effective altruism, making huge bets on behalf of many, many other people
EA culture prides itself on offering a counter to commonsense morality
The community has shown a willingness to take big risks and justify them with complex calculations
But believing you are intelligent enough to adopt a counter-intuitive, galaxy-brained strategy and end up saving the world with it often involves some hubris
And hubris makes me nervous in a field as high-stakes as AI
The idea is that if Anthropic proves it can build AI that’s both powerful and safe, the market will expect both — so other AI companies will then feel compelled to compete on safety, too

That may sound nice in theory, but it means Anthropic has to keep building ever-more-powerful AIs. “The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier,” Amodei wrote . “And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.” In other words, Amodei is sticking to his bet.  But Amodei is gambling with, by his and his company’s own telling, the future of humanity
If AI goes wrong, it could lead to our gradual disempowerment , a galling concentration of power , or even complete extinction

So there’s a very basic question that the public deserves a good answer to right at this pivotal moment: What is the evidence that Anthropic’s stated strategy — compete at the frontier so as to drive a “race to the top” — is actually successful overall? From the outside, it looks like Anthropic has done more, on balance, to drive a race to the bottom. (Disclosure: Future Perfect is funded in part by the BEMC Foundation, whose major funder was also an early investor in Anthropic; they don’t have any editorial input into our content.) In fact, part of the problem may be that Anthropic continues to treat this as a classic arms race

Specifically, the company seems to model it as a prisoner’s dilemma: If Anthropic stopped building more powerful AI, another player — whether it’s China, OpenAI, or another company — would just build it anyway
In this kind of dilemma, if the other player is going to defect, it’s rational for you to defect, even though nobody actually wants that outcome
But what if this framing misses the point?  Game theory can make a huge gamble seem sophisticated, while making the obvious alternative — just don’t build a doom machine — seem naive
Yet the fact that Anthropic and others are now racing toward RSI makes it much more likely that we could lose control of AI and start to see massive damage to our world

When the cost of defecting from safety is that you create a serious risk of catastrophic harm — or of all humanity, including you, going extinct — is that still a “rational” move?  Instead of telling yourself that you can galaxy-brain your way through this with fancy enough game theory, maybe you’re better off just thinking of this as something much simpler: Russian roulette

More and more leading voices in AI are starting to recognize that.  “We should stop AI progress now, starting unilaterally with Anthropic and/or OpenAI stopping — and then broadening out as a second step to more AI companies and negotiations with China,” Geoffrey Irving, who was until recently the chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute, told me. “Unilateral pauses can’t hold for long, but they are the right first step: When you’re doing a very dangerous thing, the correct action is stop, even if others are also doing dangerous things.” Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.  The case that Anthropic has done more harm than good Let’s be clear: The question is not whether Anthropic has done anything good on the safety front
Standing up to the Pentagon , temporarily holding back access to frontier models, and publicly advocating for safer AI policies are a few examples, among others

But the real question is whether the company’s “race to the top” strategy is working on balance — whether it’s net-negative or net-positive for safety.  Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at AI safety advocacy organization Encode, recently set off a firestorm among tech watchers, writing on X, “When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to superintelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary.” Here’s his list of what Anthropic has done: And this is all just in the past year
If we rewind the tape further back, we see Anthropic pushing back on a landmark bill to regulate AI
Rewind even further back, and we see indications that Anthropic’s core strategy may have been flawed from the start
According to Reuters , in late 2022, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman heard rumors that Anthropic was building an AI-powered chatbot
So he ordered his employees to ship an OpenAI chatbot first
The rivalry between OpenAI and Anthropic seems not only to have hastened the arrival of generative AI, but also to keep pushing release dates forward to this day

The two companies have been known to release new or cheaper models within hours of each other , each one keen to protect its market share.  Even if you think Anthropic’s behavior was justified in 2022 because publicly demonstrating the risks of AI also demonstrates the need to regulate AI — a common claim within the company and AI discourse writ large — you have to ask: Is it still justifiable now, when AI has reached this level of power and sophistication? Anthropic has indicated that it’s getting closer and closer to achieving RSI

In January, Amodei himself wrote , “I am concerned that LLMs are approaching (or may already have reached) the knowledge needed to create and release [biological weapons] end-to-end, and that their potential for destruction is very high

Some biological agents could cause millions of deaths.” And  he wrote in September, “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .” But at this point, Amodei and his staffers are themselves perhaps the primary ones accelerating the rate of AI capability development. “Anthropic seems to be doing the whole RSI thing more than anyone else, other than perhaps OpenAI,” Calvin told me. “And I just think that seems insane given their publicly stated views on the risks.”  “I think people at Anthropic should reckon more with the fact that it seems like the modal outcome is that the largest impact that Anthropic will have had is dramatically accelerating the race to RSI,” he continued. “On the current trajectory, everything else they will have done and thought and ideals they had will be a rounding error compared to their contribution there.” Anthropic should be willing to invite scrutiny on this point — and, if it believes it’s actually making the field safer than it otherwise would be, to show us the receipts
How? It could put before Congress a bill that actually strengthens safety, instead of weakening it
It could stick to its former Responsible Scaling Policy and get other companies to do the same, instead of jettisoning its commitments
It could influence other labs not to build RSI, instead of leading the charge
In the absence of such evidence, the “race to the top” logic just doesn’t hold water

title: The Supreme Court is poised to make taxpayers fund anti-LGBTQ discrimination
excerpt: On November 3, the Supreme Court will hear St
body: On November 3, the Supreme Court will hear St

Roy, which squarely presents the question of whether the Constitution authorizes discrimination by religious schools. | Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images For years, the Supreme Court has flirted with the question of whether religious conservatives may simply ignore laws prohibiting discrimination against LGBTQ Americans
The Court’s Republican majority frequently rules in favor of business owners and institutions that refuse to serve gay or trans people

But these cases often rely on ad hoc reasoning that seems designed to give religious conservatives a narrow win without resolving broader questions about whether people with anti-LGBTQ religious views have an absolute right to violate civil rights laws
On November 3, however, the Court will hear St
Roy , which squarely presents the question of whether the Constitution authorizes discrimination by religious schools
Given the Court’s past behavior in similar cases, it’s hard to imagine St
Mary ending in anything other than a victory for religious groups that wish to exclude sexual or gender minorities

The case also presents another, related question: When does the Constitution require states to subsidize religious institutions? The Republican justices’ recent decisions suggest that they are eager to make taxpayers spend a great deal more money to promote religion
The case concerns a Colorado law that pays for preschool education for all 4-year-olds in the state
Families with eligible children may choose from a broad range of private and public schools, including religious schools
But the state also bars schools that participate in this program from discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity
Religious preschools that discriminate may continue to operate in Colorado
Although Colorado does have a broad ban on anti-LGBTQ discrimination, that ban exempts places that are “ principally used for religious purposes .” So the sole issue in St
Mary is whether Colorado’s taxpayers must fund religious schools that engage in discrimination
Until fairly recently, the question of whether a state would fund religious education was up to the state itself
Simmons-Harris that states had broad leeway to decide whether to fund religious education
They could, if they chose to, set up private school voucher programs that include religious schools
But they could also choose only to fund secular education
Makin (2022), however, the Supreme Court abandoned this permissive approach
The case struck down a Maine program that offered private school tuition vouchers to students in sparsely populated areas where it was not cost-efficient for the state to operate a public school
Maine law provided that these vouchers could only be used at “nonsectarian schools,” but the Court’s Republican majority held that school voucher programs must include religious schools
The Colorado preschool program at issue in St
Mary , in contrast to the program in Maine, does not bar any school from participating because it teaches religion or is affiliated with a particular faith
The program merely requires all participating schools — be they Catholic, protestant, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, or secular — to comply with an anti-discrimination law

Mary , in other words, is whether religious schools can not only demand taxpayer funding, but also demand exemptions from generally applicable rules that apply to all other schools that accept that funding — essentially requiring taxpayers to pay for institutions that discriminate

Mary plaintiffs want the Supreme Court to join together separate lines of religion cases The Court’s Republican majority has spent more than a decade remaking how the Constitution approaches religion — or, at least, rewriting the Court’s own precedents interpreting the Constitution’s provisions governing religious rights

One of those provisions guarantees everyone the right to “free exercise” of their own faith, while the other prohibits the government from creating an “establishment of religion.” Broadly speaking, the Court’s recent decisions have read the first provision expansively , while simultaneously reducing limits on the government’s ability to advance religion — or even holding that the government is constitutionally required to fund religious institutions

Mary plaintiffs ask the Court to marry two branches of its recent religion decisions — one of which governs when people who object to a law on religious grounds are exempt from following it; the other asks when the government must fund religious schools

The first branch involves the Constitution’s free exercise clause, and this Court has fairly consistently held that, when the interests of religious conservatives conflict with LGBTQ Americans — or, really, anyone who takes a relatively liberal approach to sexuality — religious conservatives win

If you are a religious conservative, and you want an exemption from a law barring discrimination against LGBTQ people, this Court will make up a reason why you should win.  That said, while this Court consistently favors religious conservatives over queer people, the Court’s cases governing when a person of faith is exempt from a law that they object to on religious grounds are fairly incoherent and have not articulated clear legal rules

Smith (1990), the Court held that these exemptions are not available when someone challenges a “neutral law of general applicability,” meaning that the law applies with equal force to both religious and non-religious people or institutions
But Smith is, to put it mildly, not a beloved decision
Congress tried, semi-successfully , to overrule it when it enacted the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993
And the Court’s most recent religion cases often read like the justices are looking for an excuse not to follow Smith .  In Masterpiece Cakeshop v
Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018), for example, the Court ruled in favor of a Christian baker who refused to bake wedding cakes for same-sex couples

But the Court grounded that decision in facts very specific to the case, and Masterpiece Cakeshop offers judges little guidance on how they should decide other religion cases that don’t involve these unusual facts
Philadelphia (2021), the Court dodged a showdown over whether to overrule Smith and again resolved the case based on facts that were unique to that case

These are just two examples of the Court finding ways to not follow the rule it laid out in Smith , without overruling Smith or otherwise announcing a broad legal rule that governs free exercise cases

Mary plaintiffs list “at least eight different categories of cases where Smith does not control .” It appears that the Court has kept Smith in this strange limbo state — neither overruled nor followed in many cases — because several of the justices aren’t sure what legal rule should exist in its place

title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus

The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.  It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”    “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater
The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.” This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture
But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years

Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers
Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience
The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes

It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?) If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company
The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made

Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection

We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.” Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience
This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business

Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.”  In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this (although it’s pretty wild to read about machine sentience in an IPO prospectus.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum
When so little seems certain, what it says is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship
It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation

Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).   Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said
But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked

Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.  But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that
As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free

Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos
In fact, Anthropic is all of these things

As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry
The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly
And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.” Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard

There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.) Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us
They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs
They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light
But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra
Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy
In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read
This article has been updated with additional details from the IPO prospectus.

title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
excerpt: Consider what passes for success in technology policy
body: Consider what passes for success in technology policy
An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide
A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl
These are important protections, and they should have existed all along
But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling
We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day
As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms

We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.  A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases

Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching
A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines
A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions
Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation
Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line
It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms
Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address
This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states

The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services
Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed
This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable
We have been through a version of this with social media

Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there

No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale
Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war
The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world
AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance
It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to
A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people

MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete
There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects
We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place

Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own)
But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain

We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.  We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more
Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms

Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves
The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline

Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119
Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list

Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs
She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

title: Trump’s vicious closing message in Michigan
excerpt: The day after former President Barack Obama and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigned together in Detroit, President Donald Trump launched an anti
body: The day after former President Barack Obama and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigned together in Detroit, President Donald Trump launched an anti-Muslim attack against El-Sayed. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s midterm barnstorming is getting uglier and more desperate.  What’s happening? At a campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, Trump launched a new round of anti-Muslim attacks against Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, describing him as a “jihadist” who “should never be allowed inside the halls of our great beautiful Capitol.”  “If Abdul and the Democrats win,” Trump told supporters , “they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.” What’s the context? Trump’s speech marks the crescendo — so far — of what has become an increasingly Islamophobic midterm campaign by the Republican Party, centered on El-Sayed

Mike Rogers, Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee, has repeatedly tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, and Republicans have also attempted to wield Islamophobia against the Democratic Party as a whole
Greg Abbott told Fox News that his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, “supports Sharia law,” while at the Republican midterm convention in September, Texas Sen
Ted Cruz said that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans

What’s the big picture? In addition to his overt Islamophobia, Trump’s presence on the campaign trail in the final few weeks of the midterm elections has been decidedly strange and surprisingly heavy on physical descriptions of Sen

Jon Husted (R-OH) .  Now, with just eight days to go, Trump’s itinerary features rallies in Mississippi, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Florida — all Republican states where the party has found itself, to one degree or another, with a tougher-than-expected Senate race on its hands.  It’s hardly the travel schedule of a president who feels good about his party’s chances— such as in Michigan, where El-Sayed is leading in most recent polls
And with that, it’s time to log off… US elections may not be until next week, but two other countries held theirs over the weekend: Serbia and Brazil

As my colleague Caitlin Dewey reports in Vox’s Today, Explained newsletter , both resulted in surprise victories over right-wing nationalist parties, with Serbia ousting its incumbent strongman, Aleksandar Vučić

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory over Flávio Bolsonaro is also especially good news for the climate: As the New York Times reported earlier this month, the fate of the Amazon rainforest may well have hinged on the outcome of the election
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!
